doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Intellectual snobbery and finding swing tenor players inaccessible
summary: Mandel explains why Lockjaw Davis and Jimmy Forrest left him cold in the late sixties while AACM concerts at the University of Chicago excited him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You mentioned being, you considered yourself an intellectual—
An intellectual snob. Okay. Do you think that people, the general listening audience connects being intellectual snobs with jazz?

I mean I think that there’s this mythology that you have to know everything about jazz or jazz is some sort of heady music that is not accessible readily. I’ve never understood that exactly. I mean it’s so dramatic. I can understand it, when I would go to hear music by some of the aging, really the swing masters: Jimmy Forrest, Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis, guys like this. Now they were a little bit past their prime I supposed by the time I was hearing them in the late sixties. And they did not represent what I considered the avante garde. They were not taking structural chances. They were not playing the extremes of their horn. I didn’t hear the vocalization in that that I’d heard in the “Art Ensemble.” And I should backtrack a little bit. It was a matter of circumstance that I grew up near the University of Chicago where a lot of the AACM experimentation was being done, so it was someplace that I could go for an evening, my parents let me out with the car and we had moved to the northern suburbs, I didn’t have any friends there, my friends were still on the south side, so it was someplace that I could meet or go to be near my previous home was the University of Chicago concert. So I heard Roscoe Mitchell and Lester Bowie and Muhal Richard Abrams. But then at the same time I thought well that’s jazz and then here’s this other jazz going on, Joe Siegel would put on Sunday afternoon concerts of these older swing tenor players, swing to bop tenor players. And I didn’t understand it, it didn’t attract me. It was a lot of notes. You know, the constant stream of eighth notes, sixteenth notes. I didn’t hear the melodies being played. I didn’t hear them pausing. It seemed to me that the songs were all very similar. The solos did not partake of the melody, they partook of the changes I learned later. But it just felt like they were running changes. And to me, that is inaccessible to the general audience. They do not understand why that’s interesting. The notes seem even and consistent but they’re not

making melodies, they’re just making a lot of notes. And the interaction there, although I think the jazz people understand very well the kind of interaction that’s going on, I think to the listener who’s not exposed in a deep way, it sounds pro forma. And you do not hear the interaction between the drummer and the saxophonist and the pianist who’s comping for the soloist. You don’t hear it as something that’s being created afresh. Now again, maybe it’s because these guys were a little bit past their prime, they didn’t have the fire.
